newsitem.title: UK: U.S. Treasuries gain in London on short-covering.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries gain in London on short-covering.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries gained in London on Tuesday as investors switched out of European debt in favour of buying the U.S., traders said.
There was also some short covering, as many traders went short ahead of the long weekend, when U.S. markets were closed for a partial holiday on Monday.
"Everyone is nervous of shorting this market," said a trader at a French bank in London. "It's like a runaway train, and no-one wants to be left behind."
The U.S. 30-year long bond was at 101-08, yielding 6.53 percent, by 1100 GMT.
That compared with 101-04 in Tokyo and 101-08 in New York on Friday. March T-bond futures settled at 113-30 on Friday.
Traders said there was little direct news to hold the market's attention, which was leading to speculation about such issues as the health of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.
China played down fears over his health, which is rumoured to have deteriorated after a stroke, saying that there had been no major change in the condition of the 92-year old.

David Hewitt, bond strategist at Tokyo Mitsubishi said that investors were looking to U.S assets for yield, since benchmark 10-year Bunds broke through the 5.5 percent barrier at the end of last week.
"They have now consolidated that break and are around 5.45 percent," he said.
The trader said he had also seen investors switching out of BTPs in favour of Treasuries.
Hewitt noted that the three- to ten-year U.S. spread was at 36 basis points, within one basis point of its lowest level for six months.
"The curve has significantly flattened since the refunding," he said. "Retail demand is more at the short end than the long end. People don't want to chase the long end rally."
The 10-year benchmark bond was trading at 99-01, to yield 6.383 percent, while 3-year T-notes were at 99-31 to yield 5.886 percent.
